utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Ms. Tecla Henry-Benjamin, Mr. Mathias Neuner, Daryl Mundis, and our case manager, Mr. Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And could we have the appearances for the Defence. They're all present.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Muriel Cauvin, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to greet everyone present, the Prosecution, the Defence, the accused, and everyone else in the courtroom. We have to render our oral decision now. I will first ask the registrar to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. First of all, I would like to make sure that you can hear the interpretation of my words into a language that you can understand. If that is the case, can you please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, loud and clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called as a Prosecution witness. You have to make a solemn declaration. Before that, I have to identify you; therefore, I am kindly asking you to give us your first name, your last name, the date and place of birth, and your nationality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Henk Morsink. I was born at 15th of May, 1956. I was born in the place of Enschede. My nationality is Dutch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see you're wearing a military uniform. What is your rank in the Dutch Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My rank is colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, have you ever testified before either an international tribunal or a national court about the events which took place in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I testified twice in the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember the case in which you appeared as a witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The first case was the case of Mr. Blaskic, and the second case was the case of Mr. Kordic and Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In these two cases, were you called as a Prosecution witness or as a Defence witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was called as a Prosecution witness in both cases, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, what was your position? What was your rank in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My position was a monitor for the European Union. I was not wearing my rank at that time. I was a major in the Dutch Army, but I had the position of a diplomat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could you now please read the solemn declaration that the usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is your third appearance before this Tribunal, so you are used to the procedure. That's why I'm going to be very brief. First of all, you are going to be asked questions by the Prosecution, then by the Defence. The Defence is going to ask you questions to check your credibility as a witness and to set the context of the events which took place. After that, the Prosecution will have to -- the right to re-examine you, and the Judges which are before you can also put questions to you at any point in time when they deem necessary to do so. Please be as complete in your answers as possible, because as you know, we are conducting an oral procedure here and what is important here is the oral debate and your words carry a lot of weight. I would like to point out two other elements: You have taken the solemn declaration, which means that you will be telling the truth. False testimony before this Tribunal is against the law and may be punishable. In case you don't want to answer a question because the answer might incriminate you, the Chamber may compel you to answer such a question; however the Chamber will guarantee you a form of immunity. In very general words, this is how the procedure before this Tribunal is going to take place. The Prosecution can also ask you questions about the documents that you might have delivered to the investigators, but I leave it to the Prosecution to clarify this, because we have to be really very clear on the point of the documents that you have delivered. Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel Morsink.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Trial Chamber, can you please briefly describe your military career from the time you joined the Dutch Army up to the present.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I joined the Dutch Army in 1976. I joined the military academy in Breda for four years, then I was appointed as a lieutenant, as a platoon leader of a tank platoon. I stayed with that same battalion for eight years in various functions. After that, in 1988 I was invited to go to the Dutch general staff course. I completed that course. Then I was appointed as a brigade operations and training officer, S3 officer, for three years. At the end of that job, I was sent as a monitor to Bosnia-Herzegovina within the ECMM structure. Immediately after my return from Bosnia, I was invited to go to the German general staff college in Hamburg for two years. I finished that course as well. After that, I was appointed as a lieutenant colonel in The Hague in the Army Staff for almost three years. After that, I got my own command over a tank battalion for two years. I handed over command in early 2000. I was appointed as the chief, present information of the Dutch Army here in The Hague. And after that, I was appointed for almost two and a half Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. years as the chief cabinet of the Dutch Army Chief of Staff. And since last year June, I am appointed as the chief, plans and policy in the German Netherlands Corps headquarters in Munster, Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel, you told us, as you've told the Chamber previously, that you were part of the ECMM structure in Bosnia. When were you first given that assignment?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The assignment started at the 13th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when did that assignment conclude?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The assignment concluded exactly three months later, at the 13th of July, also 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what type of background briefings, if any, you received prior to taking this assignment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Dutch Army organised a training prior to missions like monitors within the ECMM and also for observers within the United Nations military observing mission. This training consisted of a two weeks' training here in The Hague at the Clingendael Institute. These two weeks - in fact, ten working days - included ethical background, historical background, religious background, some techniques about how to negotiate, how to chair things like joint commissions. After these two weeks, I got some additional training, military training on how to handle mines and unexploded ordnances and some first-aid additional training. And upon arrival in Zagreb on the 13th of April, I received approximately one and a half days information about the current situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, about communications used by the ECMM, and in addition again about first aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel, when you say you received information about the current situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, can you please elaborate a little bit. What do you mean by "the current situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina"?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: In Zagreb, we -- all the new monitors attended a daily briefing and we got an additional briefing on the entire situation in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I recall this was quite common. At the end of that briefing, I learnt that I was to go to Zenica and I recall that details about Zenica were very few.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell us how you got from Zagreb to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Initially, it was planned to go by helicopter, but it appeared to be unsafe or the weather might not have been okay. So in the end, in the morning I learnt that I had to go by car towards Split, and we arrived one day later Split and then actually flew by helicopter to Kiseljak, and from Kiseljak I was picked up by an ECMM car and was brought to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, do you recall the date that you actually arrived in Zenica and the approximate time?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The helicopter arrived in Kiseljak close before sunset, so in April that must have been, I think, 1900 hours. I was picked up and drove in darkness to Zenica, so I guess I arrived there maybe 2100 hours, maybe half past 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the exact date in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The date was the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell us about the first day, that is the 17th of April, 1993, what type of additional information you received about your assignment, your duties, and any briefings that you received on the 17th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Again, the information was very little. I expected to hear at least what they -- what the leadership there expected from me. But in the morning briefing - not a well-structured morning briefing, I must say - I learnt that together with another monitor I was to go to Vitez and we were escorted by two British armoured vehicles. And in Vitez for the first time I learned exactly what was going on in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber a little bit about the ECMM structure, chain of command, and number of monitors that were in the field at the time you arrived.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The structure was that the headquarters of the ECMM was in Zagreb and there was a regional centre directly in the chain of command under this headquarters in Zagreb, a regional centre in Zenica, chaired by Mr. Thebault, whom we addressed as the ambassador. He had a small staff, a chief of staff, Mr. Bis [phoen], and a number of monitors which I think was approximately 15. I'm not sure. Maybe 10 or 15 at that time. And these monitors were supported by a supporting staff of drivers and administrative supporters, and the regional centre had some interpreters in service as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Upon your arrival, what was your primary duty or responsibility?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I was sent as a team member to the Vitez area. I was informed there by senior team members and by other monitors. All in total I think there were four monitors in the Vitez area. And our first mission was to find out about the actual situation on the ground in Vitez, to get information, to try to make contact with the HVO side in Vitez, and the Armija BiH side in Vitez, and finally to try to broker a cease-fire to be able to coordinate humanitarian assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, you told us you were sent as a team member to the Vitez area. Do you recall the names of any of the other members of the team that you were a part of in this Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Mr. Erik Friis-Pedersen, a Danish monitor; he was quite senior to me. Mr. Torbjorn Junhov, a Swedish monitor; and Mr. Remi Landry, a Canadian monitor. And there was one Danish monitor as well whom I'm not sure whether it was Allan Laustsen or maybe Lars Baggesen, one of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the three-month period that you were with ECMM in Central Bosnia, did your responsibilities or the area you covered change in any way?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, it did. Since I was a junior monitor, they gave me some time to gain experience in the region. Based on the example of the Busovaca Joint Commission, which was raised earlier prior to my arrival, we started a similar local joint commission in the Vitez area and later on we expanded this example to Busovaca, Kiseljak, and the Travnik -- the larger Travnik area. So in total, I worked in four local joint commissions, and after I gained some experience, I was asked to chair those commissions, and I later on attended the coordinating centre in Travnik as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, did you receive any briefings at any time you were in Central Bosnia from BritBat or did you have any contact with any information or intelligence officers from BritBat?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. Since we had our ECMM house fairly close to the British Battalion in the small village of Bila and since we had to work fairly closely together with the British officers, we exchanged information almost on a daily basis and I saw the British Battalion intelligence officer, the so-called S2 officer, at least once a week, sometimes more often. I gave him information, my findings at those meetings, and he gave me information in exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, do you recall the name of the S2 officer at BritBat that you met with on these occasions?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At any point in time did this BritBat S2 officer provide you with any documents?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. Quite early during my stay in that region - it might have been the end of the first or maybe the second week - he handed three org charts to me showing the organisation of the 3rd Corps of the Armija BiH with the brigades and names of brigade commanders on it and the numbers of the brigade and a similar org chart of the operational zone middle Bosnia of the HVO side and a somewhat more detailed one about the -- I think about the Zenica organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on this information or the other briefings that you received, what information, if any, did you have about the presence of foreign fighters in Central Bosnia? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: On this org chart about the 3rd Corps Armija BiH there was a brigade called the 7th Muslim Brigade and there was a note about this brigade that foreign members -- foreign soldiers or foreign citizens were a member of this brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time you were in Central Bosnia, did you ever encounter or see any of these foreign fighters?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't recall any personal contact with foreign fighters, but I was told several times by fellow monitors that they were present in that area. And I was told by one of my senior fellow monitors during one of the introductions - I think it was during one of the travels from Zenica to Vitez - to stay away from a certain area in Zenica because there were supposed to be foreign fighters or the 7th Muslim Brigade in that area and it was supposed to be unsafe for monitors to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, do you have any recollection today of what area in Zenica your colleague was referring to?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I could point it out on the map, but as far as I know, it is the southern side of Zenica, close to the Bosna River and the road where it crosses the Bosna River, if you drive to the Busovaca junction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On how many occasions did you ever see any of these foreign soldiers or foreign citizens in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I think in very few occasions. I recall one very well, and that's the exchange of prisoners. But I must say they -- I could not recognise them as called the Mujahedins at that time, since they were wearing sports suits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You've mentioned the exchange of prisoners. Do you recall the approximate date or dates that you're make reference to?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The date is the middle of June. I think it was the middle of May. I think the 17th of May the actual exchange took place in the afternoon, in the late afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel, we'll return to that prisoner exchange a little bit later. Before we do, you've made reference to a number of commissions that you were involved with during the time that you were in Central Bosnia as an ECMM monitor. Can you please tell us why these joint commissions were established. What was their purpose?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Their purpose was to try to bring together the commanders of both parties, the HVO side and the Armija BiH side, on a local level to try to negotiate cease-fires if possible; to deal with violations against the agreed cease-fire on higher levels; to coordinate and organise humanitarian assistance, and under that I count the names of exchange of prisoners, if possible, the release of prisoners, exchange of missing people, trying to solve those problems of missing people, coordinating the exchange of wounded people, escort them from hospital to hospital. So a range of humanitarian jobs to be done in the region on the local level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel, you've made reference that the fact that the commission's -- one of the purposes was to bring together the commanders of both parties. Do you recall the specific individuals who attended these commission meetings?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. I recall a number of them. In Vitez, they started with the brigade commander on the HVO side, Mr. Cerkez; and on the Armija BiH side the brigade concerning Vitez was split into a battalion commanded by Sivro Cifet, he was located in Kruscica. And the brigade commander -- the actual brigade commander was Mr. Kelestura. These both commanders appointed liaison officers, Mr. Jozic and Mr. Hajdarevic, and they regularly attended the local joint commission Vitez. In Busovaca, it was Mr. Grubisic of the HVO side and Mr. Mekic of the Armija BiH side. They were almost all the time accompanied by three or four local assistants. I don't recall the names. I don't recall any names from Kiseljak. And in the Travnik area, we had several, let's say, local commissions, all called, let's say, the larger region of Travnik. One was covering Nova Bila. One was covering the Han Bila and Guca Gora area, and sometimes there was a meeting in Travnik itself. I don't know -- I don't recall all the names. And I must say that from the top level Mr. Merdan from the Armija BiH side and Mr. Nakic from the HVO side were, at least in the beginning, always present to support the process of setting up these local joint commissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say, sir, that Mr. Merdan and Mr. Nakic were always present at least in the beginning, at which location or locations were they always present?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The first meetings in Vitez started in the ECMM house, close to the British Battalion. They were present there. Mr. Merdan even spent the night there sometimes. Mr. Nakic used to go home, because he lived close by this facility. The location in Busovaca was in the beginning the Dutch transportation -- the headquarters of the Dutch transportation battalion in the so-called Hotel Nunspeet [phoen]. The location in Kiseljak was at the Canadian base. And the location in Han Bila was in a school, I think one of the local military facilities, not being a UN or ECMM facility; and the same goes for Nova Bila. This was also one of the headquarters of one of the both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel, you've told us that Mr. Merdan and Mr. Nakic attended the meetings in Vitez. Do you recall whether they attended meetings in any of the other locations you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Merdan and Nakic both joined several meetings in Busovaca and in Kiseljak and also in Han Bila. I don't recall any presence of them in Nova Bila, but by that time the so-called joint command in Travnik in the PTT building was raised and their attention and their appearance in that headquarters was necessary, and the work more or less accelerated on the local basis, so their presence was not always needed any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel, can you recall approximately how many times during the three-month period that you were in Central Bosnia you personally attended any of these commission meetings?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: This was almost on a daily basis. Sometimes even two meetings took place at one day. But we had certain periods where the work didn't go that well, so my estimate is that altogether maybe 50 meetings took place which I attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please give the Trial Chamber a rough approximation as to the number of meetings that Mr. Merdan and Mr. Nakic would have attended out of that rough number of 50 that you attended.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: If I don't count the meetings of the joint command, since they are something different than the local joint commissions, I would say Mr. Merdan and Mr. Nakic both attended maybe 20 meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What time period during the three-month period you were in Central Bosnia were these commissions operating?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I think the first real operational joint commission started early May, the beginning of May, maybe the 4th or the 5th of May, and some of the commissions were still operational when I left Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I take it from your answer that some of them were still operational. Does that mean that some of them were not?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right. We had a fallback in Vitez and we had a fallback in the Han Bila area as well, sometimes due to the military situation; sometimes due to what I would like to call a political interference. The Vitez Joint Commission fell apart because the military was no longer willing or able to join and the local politicians tried to take over but didn't fully accept our role in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, you just mentioned local politicians attempting to take over at some point these joint commissions or commissions. In the early days of the commissions, what involvement, if any, did the political leaders have in these commissions?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: In the early days, they had no direct interference or influence, at least not that I noticed, because only officers or soldiers attended the meetings. I had separate meetings or discussions with local politicians in Vitez. In Busovaca, it more or less developed automatically when there -- when we started to get a certain level of understanding between both parties. They both suggested that the mayor of both sides and especially the religious representatives of both sides, so the priest and the imam, should join these meetings and try to more or less ease the tension.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What involvement, if any, did the civilian police or Ministry of the Interior officials have in these joint commissions?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't recall any direct interference or influence of the civil police. Maybe through the mayor. I'm not sure. Military police might have had some influence through commanders, but they were not present during the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate time frame when the local civilian authorities, the mayors, for example, in Busovaca became involved?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That must have been in the middle of May, late May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than in the Busovaca area, how much involvement did civilian authorities have in the joint commissions?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: They had hardly any influence, apart from Travnik. But I must say that the meetings in Travnik that took place end of May, early June were on a provincial level, since the ECMM tried to support the province number 10 in the Vance-Owen Plan and of course a lot of politicians were present at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's return now to a more general issue. I'd like to ask you some questions about the state of preparedness of the parties for these meetings. Do you have any general comments about how prepared the parties were at the actual meetings themselves?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: In the beginning, they were not prepared or badly prepared, but they learnt quite quickly because there was a sense of urgency on both sides. They showed the willingness to solve problems and they realised, I think, that to be able to solve problems you should prepare yourself for meetings. And the best example is that they had quite accurate lists of detainees, accurate lists of missing people, of wounded people, what people are in which hospital, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you elaborate a little bit on the accurate -- you've said "quite accurate lists of detainees." Can you elaborate on that or perhaps give us some examples of what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: A usual question during those meetings was one of the parties started listing a list of missing people, and in quite some occasions there was an immediate reaction from the other side stating that he knew where a number of those people were. For instance, they were taken to a certain prison, or they could state that they were in hospital. And that left us with only a few names still missing after such a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether what you've just told us applied to one side to the party or to both sides? That is, were both sides equally prepared or was one side more prepared than the other?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I think both sides were more or less equally prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Colonel Morsink, based on what you observed, what kind of records was it that the parties maintained to prepare for these meetings.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Specific records were lists of missing people and lists of detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How much information was contained in these specific records, as you've characterised them?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: These lists normally were numbered. Every serial line was numbered. They contained the names, the surnames, and the name of birth, the year of birth, sometimes even the date of birth, and sometimes the place of birth. And these lists were all, almost always, officially stamped and signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What did the parties do with these documents at the commission meetings?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Most of the times they gave a copy to the other side and a copy to the ECMM, and I saved some of those copies. And then they discussed the contents of the list and sometimes, if they were not complete enough or questions were left, they agreed on solving those questions in the next meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you characterise for the Trial Chamber the atmosphere or ambiance at these meetings, in terms of were they agitated, calm. How did the parties react these meetings?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It's hard to say. It was not a general atmosphere. It depends on the situation. If there was a cease-fire during the night or the day before, then they tend to be quite agitated. Both sides took the opportunity to explain historical background again and again to explain exactly from their point of view what happened during that cease-fire violation. And then after a certain period I tend to chair the meeting and to ask them exactly what they wanted to achieve during the meeting, and then the exchange of information started. It appeared to me that commanders knew each other from the past, at least the liaison officers in the Vitez local commission knew each other quite well. And I have pictures where the -- both brigade commanders from the Busovaca area sit together on a couch and communicate quite normally as if there wasn't any fighting at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, were you aware of any communications between the liaison officers or the participants in the meeting and individuals up their own respective chains of command?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. I'm quite sure that they had good communications internally. For instance, liaison officer Mr. Refik Hajdarevic, he lived in Poculica and if we made an agreement to give additional information in the next meeting, then he would -- he showed himself able to get this additional information and he would never have done it without good communications, either by travelling personally or by calling. And the same goes for the other side, although the distances were much shorter for the HVO side, since the liaison officer was dropped off at the headquarters of the HVO brigade in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, you've mentioned Refik Hajdarevic. Whom did Mr. Hajdarevic represent?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: He was appointed by the brigade commander of the Armija BiH brigade in the Vitez area. The headquarters was in Preocica, and I think his name was -- I said it earlier. It will come back to my mind again, but I don't know -- I don't recall the name right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Which of the warring parties did Mr. Hajdarevic belong to?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: He belonged to the Armija BiH side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about -- you've mentioned that the liaison officer was dropped off at the headquarters. Can you tell us a little bit about any other efforts that ECMM or any other international organisation provided with respect to logistics, for these meetings?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The meetings were chaired by the ECMM. They were hosted sometimes by the ECMM, sometimes by the UN, either the British Battalion or the Canadian or the Dutch Battalion. And the transport, if necessary, was organised by the British liaison officers that took part in the meetings as well, and they most of the times used British armoured vehicles since representatives had to cross front lines more than once and it was not safe to travel in an unsecure vehicle or even travel in their own private vehicles. For the Kiseljak area, the Canadian Battalion would support those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel, do you recall any specific instances where transportation was provided for members of the ABiH to any of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Merdan was picked up regularly in Zenica by a British vehicle, sometimes at the headquarters of the 3rd Corps Armija BiH. The representatives in Busovaca were picked up in Kacuni and had to cross the front line to go to Busovaca. And Mr. Hajdarevic and Mr. Sivro Sifet coming from Kruscica were picked up by British vehicles as well to be able to go to the Vitez ECMM house and the same goes for the area of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, are you aware of any instance where either of the parties at any of these joint commissions were acting independently of their respective chains of command?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Maybe a first reaction during a meeting might have been independently. But I had the impression during all meetings that there was enough back-brief between local commanders and their superiors. Certainly liaison officers didn't have full authority. They had to back-brief their commanders on a daily basis and to gain, let's say, limited authority for the next meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What do you base this impression on? What factors led you to this impression?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The results of the local commission meetings lead me to this impression. And for the case of commanders, I think they were -- they had the authority to make decisions of themselves, like the brigade commanders in the Busovaca area. They decided at the spot on exchange of people, on freedom of movement for small numbers of people. And the same goes for Mr. Merdan and Nakic as well -- they showed enough authority to be able to answer difficult questions, to explain situations, and to make decisions on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know based on discussions you had with Mr. Merdan about the extent of his ability to answer difficult questions or to explain situations?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: He explained situations, but not always he could explain things right on the spot. He -- sometimes he had to come back on a certain matter in the next meeting, so apparently he had to gain additional information in his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, you mentioned earlier a prisoner exchange in mid-May. Can you tell us a little bit about what role if any you played in arranging that prisoner exchange.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That one prisoner exchange you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, the one you referred to earlier in mid-May 1993.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I recall that I heard, let's say, first indications or rumours about a large prisoner exchange dealing with an important member of the HVO from one side and some other HVO soldiers and dealing with Mujahedins from the other side. But detailed information I received during one of the evening briefings in the ECMM headquarters in Zenica. I took note of these informations. I played a minor role in it. I was one of the team members to check on one of the three locations where these exchanges were organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the meetings where these exchanges were organised and the approximate date of any such meetings?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I was not present at the meetings prior to this exchange. Only this one I just mentioned, the evening briefing in the headquarters of the ECMM. And the actual exchange itself took place, I think, on the 17th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of the individuals who were involved in this exchange?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I do recall some of them, the persons I know personally. Mr. Remi Landry was appointed to organise things in Zenica during the exchange. I myself and Mr. Schellschmidt, a German monitor, were sent to Busovaca to organise the exchange there. I recall that Mr. Merdan was as a representative of the Armija BiH side, was sent to Travnik to arrange things. With me in Busovaca there was Major Mike Buffini, a British liaison officer. I recall that Mrs. Mary Jo Blanc from the ICRC was present in Busovaca. And I know from the notes that there were more people, but I don't recall their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall anyone else from the ABiH other than Mr. Merdan?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Not by name, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You've told us that there were three locations. Can you briefly explain to the Chamber how this was going to work and what was happening at each of these three locations.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I must say I only focussed on that location where I was ordered to go to; that's Busovaca. And the other two locations were the regional headquarters in Zenica itself, so the hotel, the ECMM hotel in the centre of Zenica; and the third location was the location of the joint command in Travnik, that was the PTT building at that time. At those locations a certain group of people, detainees held by a certain party, were supposed to be brought to by that party that held them detained. Checks had to be made by a number of organisations, by the ECMM at all three locations, by BritBat at all three locations, and by ICRC, and in addition to that, by liaison officers or representatives of both the HVO and the Armija BiH. So all in total, that is five independent checks at all three locations. If these checks were okay and confirmed to be okay by everybody, then the actual exchange would take part and that phase of the operation was that the detainees would be taken with armoured vehicles of the British Battalion to a next location and that would conclude the whole exchange of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, can you tell us exactly what you did on the day of the exchange. What was your role? Where did you go? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: In the morning, I had a meeting to have local Joint Commission Busovaca. That's my job. And the exchange started at midday, at noon. I had to report to the Mediapan factory. That's a wood processing factory close to Busovaca. When I arrived there, the 13 people that were supposed to be there at that location were already present. I counted those people, and I recall from a picture that I have from that situation that also the ICRC and the British Battalion were present with armoured vehicles and their liaison vehicle. And I recall from my notes that both the HVO side and the Armija BiH side were present with their representatives as well. So the whole thing was as planned. I counted the people. I reported it together with my fellow monitor to the headquarters through our own ECMM communications and so did the ICRC and the British Battalion. After that, we had to wait quite long. And in the end of the afternoon, the actual exchange took place in that way that the British Battalion was ordered to transport the 13 persons to Zenica. I did not take part in that transportation. I stayed in the Busovaca area to release a number of prisoners from the Kaonik prison, which was not directly linked to this exchange but it more or less set the ground for, let's say, a positive opportunity to free these people as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. I do have one question and it will complete this area of my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, these 13 people, can you recall what they look like? Can you describe their physical appearance and what they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I recall that they sat in one of the buildings of the factory, I think they sat on a pile of wood, all 13 in a group together. I do not recall any uniforms. I do recall a number of sports outfits, training suits of a colour that I wouldn't have chosen myself, more like a female colour, not -- from my belief, not fitting to those young people. I think the average age was early 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel Morsink.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is almost 10.30. We are going to make a break, and we shall resume around five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, I have just a couple questions concerning the people, again, that you saw at the exchange. These 13 people, were they local people or were they foreigners?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't exactly remember their faces, but I recall that some of them at least looked like not European.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You also told us that they were wearing sports outfits. Do you know where those sports outfits came from?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I'm not certain. I guess they were issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Apparently by those persons that held them detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I should also state, sir, that during the break I was asked by the interpreters if we could both slow down and also pause between question and answer. I know that that would be greatly appreciated by the interpreters. You told us, Colonel Morsink, that you were at meetings or a large number of meetings with Mr. Merdan. Can you give us your impressions of him as a military leader, based on your contact with him.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It's difficult to say something about military leadership if you only meet people in meetings and not seeing them act with their subordinate soldiers, but from what I learnt from Mr. Merdan was that he was well aware of military structures; he had apparently a lot of information on what was happening on the ground, on the battlefield; and I learnt that he was quite effective in a military way in preparing himself for meetings, preparing the liaison officers for meetings. And he also showed a lot of authority when local commanders were not willing or didn't show enough willingness to live up to the cease-fire agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on your attendance at these meetings and your observations, did Mr. Merdan have the ultimate authority to issue orders concerning prisoner exchanges?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether that goes for prisoner exchanges, but I don't think that he had the ultimate authority, since he was a deputy commander of the corps. I don't recall that he signed official papers himself. If there were official papers, then they were normally signed by Mr. Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you know, Colonel Morsink, what type of communications systems did Mr. Merdan have, based on what you observed?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Only in a few occasions I observed actual communications by Mr. Merdan or other Armija BiH corps staff members. That was in the ECMM house in Vitez when they stepped aside, used small -- I think it was a kind of a radio. It looked like a large cell phone. And apparently they used it in their own language to call maybe their headquarters, maybe somebody else, a subordinate. I'm not sure. I couldn't understand, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You've told us earlier, Colonel Morsink, about the joint command in Travnik. Can you provide the Trial Chamber with some background and information based on what you know about the joint command in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. First ideas for a joint command came to my knowledge late April, when the -- I think the top level of both armies decided for a cease-fire and also decided on how to work together or how to continue cooperation and based on this common aim for both sides, they decided, as far as I know, with support of the top politician -- political leaders, they decided to establish a so-called joint command or a joint operational command, and that was supposed to be in the PTT building, in the cellar of the PTT building in Travnik with I think a total of five or six representatives from both sides, so a total of 10 or 12 officers permanently in this joint command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, you've mentioned late April. Can you tell us what year? Again, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Late April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On how many occasions, if at all, did you enter the basement of the PTT building where this joint command headquarters was located?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Since it became operational, I think around maybe the 10th or the 12th of May. I visited it at least three or four times a week, certainly for the first month. Later on, I think after mid-June, I don't recall that I actually visited this joint command and I'm not sure whether it was still operational at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You've told us that there were five or six representatives from both sides. Do you recall the names or positions of any of the individuals on the ABiH side at that joint command headquarters?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Mr. Merdan was -- I'm not sure whether he was a permanent member of the joint command, but he -- I met him several times at the joint command. Mr. Alagic was present a number of times. I don't recall whether he was a permanent member or not. And I think the rest were staff officers from the corps staff level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the joint command?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The purpose as I learned it was to find, as they called it, their mutual enemy. They tried to continue to hold together the front lines against the Bosnian Serb army, especially in the Travnik area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, you've mentioned Mr. Alagic. Do you know what position Mr. Alagic held at the time you were in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Alagic was the commander of the operational zone in the Travnik region of the Armija BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, if you know, what an operational zone is.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: We don't know -- or we don't use these terms in Western armies. We used to refer to it as a division-type unit, a division level. And I base that on the fact that he had several brigades under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, are you familiar with the term or have you heard the term "operational group"?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. I have. And I guess that operational zone goes more for the HVO side and operational group is more applicable for the BiH side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than at the joint command headquarters, did you at any other time encounter Mr. Alagic anywhere else in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. I met him several times in his own headquarters in Travnik, in the barracks in Travnik. I met him in the field several times. He joined a small number of meetings of local joint commissions in Novi Travnik and in Han Bila that was, I think. He joined me and some others during a visit to Guca Gora, and I met him in the town hall in Travnik several times when the politicians of the province number 10 tried to start up a common provincial government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel, you mentioned that you met Mr. Alagic in his headquarters in the barracks in Travnik. Do you know which headquarters that was?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I only recall one big barracks in Travnik, and it was only a few hundred metres from the big hospital in Travnik and only a few hundred metres from the Hotel Orient where the ECMM had their temporary headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, sir, was this the operational group headquarters that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, to my knowledge it was. And there were also one or two military units based in that barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, during the period of time that you were in Central Bosnia, can you characterise the operational tempo of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: If I would refer to, length say, high-intensity war fighting like we've been preparing for in Western Europe for a number of years, the tempo in Bosnia was quite low, but in small time frames, in certain days or weeks, the tempo could rise to quite high, but in a very limited area. So it was local intense fighting and then very low intensity ongoing fighting for the rest of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel Morsink.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no further questions in direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. As far as the notebooks are concerned, Prosecution, has Ms. Benjamin been able to inform you about the results of her research?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Indeed she has, Mr. President, and I conveyed that information to the Defence at the beginning of the recess which just ended. I can certainly inform the Trial Chamber or perhaps the Defence can raise the issue directly with the witness. I leave it to you, Your Honour. I can certainly inform you as to what I have been informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Very well, Mr. Mundis. I am giving the floor to the Defence for their cross-examination. I would like to remind you that the examination-in-chief lasted exactly 59 minutes or 1 hour, so the Defence will have an hour and a half for their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, as far as the cross-examination and the duration of the cross-examination, we will need one hour and 30 minutes, and I believe that my colleagues will need about 15 or 20 minutes. I would like to bring the Chamber's attention to the fact that I have confirmed this information with the witness, the witness who is today before the Trial Chamber and who has testified in two other cases. The first -- in the first case, he testified for over 20 hours, and in the second case he testified over 7 hours. The witness has delivered more than 50 documents during the three months that he spent in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I know that we have to economise on time, but in the interest of justice we need to speed up the process. And even if I limit my questions, I will need an hour and a half to complete my cross-examination. I believe that this is necessary and reasonable within the circumstances, and I can't even touch upon the documents that have been drafted by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. You may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel. We've had the opportunity of meeting last night, and I wish to begin by taking this opportunity for expressing my appreciation for you in accepting to meet us last night. For the record, Colonel, even though we did meet last night, I would like to introduce myself and my colleagues this morning. I'm accompanied by Mrs. Edina Residovic and by Mrs. Muriel Cauvin, and together we represent General Hadzihasanovic. Colonel, we had this discussion yesterday, and I'd like to simply go back over some of the issues we covered last night. I would like to begin with a few general questions. First to confirm that you were an ECMM monitor for a period of three months, namely from 13th of April to 13th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that you were attached for the duration of this three months to the Regional Centre Zenica, which was headed by Ambassador Thebault.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And during this period, you were away from the theatre of operations for a short period, from the 10th to the 16th of June, where you were away on rest and recreation.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: As far as previous statement, can you confirm that you initially gave a first statement to the Office of the Prosecution in December of 1996?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And following which you testified both in the Blaskic in 1999 and then in the Kordic case in the year 2000, both times as a Prosecution witness?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you confirm, Colonel, that with respect to your involvement in the Blaskic case, the preparation time that you personally spent with the Office of the Prosecution, in addition to the time spent by the investigators, was somewhere around five to six days?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that your testimony lasted three full days, which would account for somewhat more than 20 hours of testimony?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I'm not a hundred per cent sure about that, but that's my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And with respect to your involvement in the Kordic case, can you confirm that the preparation time, again in addition to having provided a statement, lasted for three to four days?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that your testimony in this case lasted a little over one full day?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And one full day in those times were from morning until late in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, Colonel, we -- you showed us two small notebooks as well as one large notebook that you had prepared while you were in Bosnia as an ECMM monitor.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. But one of the small notebooks is my private diary, and it was never openly shown to anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you confirm, Colonel, whether you -- to your memory and your recollection, whether this material was ever provided to the investigators or to the lawyers of the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I have shown it to the lawyers of the Prosecution earlier, during the preparation of the other cases, and to my knowledge copies of these books have -- of these notebooks have been taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now, you spent three months in Central Bosnia, and you explained to me last night that this was a policy from the Netherlands that you would only spend three months, whereas the military component from the Netherlands would spend six months.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me - and we discussed this last night - that in spending three months in a theatre of operations such as that which was in Central Bosnia, it is very difficult to get a full understanding as to what is going on in such a short period?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I think it's possible to get the understanding, but to become effective in three months, that's the tough part of such a short duration and that's why the Dutch government decided to prolong it to six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I'd like to move quickly into the exchange which was mentioned by my colleague from the Prosecution. I'm talking about the exchange on the 17th of May. First, Colonel, can you confirm that the role of the ECMM in this exchange was that of a mediator and a facilitator in liaison with the British Battalion?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I see what you mean about mediator and facilitator, but I don't see the liaison with the British Battalion, because the mediation and facilitation was meant to mediate between HVO and Armija BiH. Both sides held prisoners or detainees. And I think the British Battalion was also merely facilitating in transporting and in giving communications and in checking.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, you just mentioned that the ABiH was holding detainees, but you have no information to that effect, do you?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I didn't personally see that or was able to confirm that. The way it was presented to us by the ECMM during the 16th briefing was in -- let's say in the simple way, HVO side, Armija BiH side, with a number of detainees from both sides or both parties to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you know from the information -- well, first let me go back a bit and confirm that you yourself only became involved in this exchange a few days before.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that Ambassador Thebault, as the head of the Regional Centre Zenica, carried out most of the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that this exchange was considered by Ambassador Thebault and others as being a very sensitive issue.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: As far as the information you have on the exchange, it was all provided to you as a briefing which you attended on the 16th of May.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And on that occasion this was a briefing held the night prior to the exchange.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, this meeting was an ECMM-only meeting. There was no one else but ECMM at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: There could have been one of the British liaison officers present. I'm not sure about that. But normally these meetings were only ECMM meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this meeting was convened by Ambassador Thebault or, as you mentioned to me last night, could have been convened by the Chief of Staff of the ECMM, a gentleman called Bis.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, as far as the information -- because we went last night over your statement, and you basically know that there were three areas where this exchange was supposed to take place. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: One of these areas was the Hotel Internacional or the regional centre itself.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And a second area was the Mediapan factory, where you yourself were asked to attend.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the third area was in Travnik at the PTT building or the joint headquarters.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, as far as the sequence of events, you knew that at the Mediapan factory the people held by the HVO were supposed to appear there, you were supposed to check on them, and then they would be released when all other conditions were made right.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. But in that fact that the release would be the transport of those 13 people with British vehicles and the actual release, you could state that it's done in Busovaca or at the end when they get out of these British vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I would like to confirm with you, because this is the area where you were, on this one you have specific knowledge: When you showed up at the Mediapan factory, which was around 12.00 that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The people who were supposed to be there - we're talking about 13 people - there was 11 persons of which you had the list and 2 drivers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: These two persons, the additional persons, were on the same list as well, so it was a list of 13 with a special group of 11 and then 2 separate names, numbered as 12 and 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, these people, you knew were detained by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I did not see these people before as well, and I didn't meet them in any prison, so it's the same impression as I had about my previous statement of people being imprisoned by the Armija BiH side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you don't know who exactly held these 13 people.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right. I based my impression on what I was told during the briefing the night before and on the notes I took, to simplify, prisoners from the HVO side and, to simplify, prisoners from the Armija BiH side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The -- those persons that you met at the Mediapan factory, can you confirm that you were provided a list of those people and that there were countries mentioned on this list?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, can you also confirm that you had no information whatsoever in terms of who these people were; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you did not know when and in what circumstances they had been arrested.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct. I was only told by fellow monitors that these were supposed to be Mujahedins, as they called them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you don't know that these persons actually were arrested as soon as they entered in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you don't know either what the purpose of these persons was in coming to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you don't know if there were any previous attempts by civilian authorities to have them released from whoever was detaining them.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the other sides of the exchange, you know that there was a brigade commander from the HVO who was detained; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right. Mr. Totic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you know who was detaining Mr. Totic?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The same impression I had based on the briefing, that there were two parties holding detainees and then apparently Mr. Totic was held by the Armija BiH side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That was the information you had.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's the impression I had based on the information I got the night before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the information, in terms of there were four HVO officers who were also being held, and these four HVO officers were supposed to show up in Travnik at the PTT building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you don't know either who was holding these four people or where they were being held.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No. Just the same information, based on the briefing the night before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you yourself were accompanied by Mr. Junhov who is another ECMM monitor, and you were told to proceed to the Mediapan factory.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I think Mr. Junhov was with me early in the morning during the joint commission meeting in Busovaca, and according to the notes I took, Mr. Schellschmidt was supposed to be with me in the Mediapan factory. So that's another monitor, not Mr. Junhov, according to the notes I took.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when you were at the Mediapan factory, you reported that there was a significant delay before this group was actually released and transported by the British Battalion to Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And during this delay, you -- can you confirm that you did not speak at any time to any of the people present?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct. I didn't speak to them. I only checked once whether all 13 were present, and that's the only time I saw them. I didn't speak to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, as far as Mr. Schellschmidt, he was not with you in the morning but he was with you at the Mediapan factory. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's what I recall, based on my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when the group was released from the Mediapan factory, you actually went back to Kaonik to check on other detainees and Mr. Schellschmidt did not accompany you.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you don't know exactly where he went when the group was released.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when you proceeded to Kaonik, it was to arrange for some release of other detainees; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me proceed to another area. Prior to this exchange, Colonel, you heard rumours about Mujahedin, but as you mentioned earlier on, you had not seen any evidence of them.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't recall any personal contacts with Mujahedins, although in one of my reports I read last night, a report signed by me myself, that I have seen some green banners at one occasion. I can't remember that any more, but it's in one of my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And these green banners could have been banners of -- could have been an official flag from a unit, could have been anything; right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It could be, yes. But the green banners, from my belief, would refer to the 7th Muslim Brigade and what I was told, that possible Mujahedin would be members of this 7th Muslim Brigade. So from my belief, there could have been a relation between green flags and Mujahedins; but again, I don't recall any personal contact with any Mujahedins.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this, Colonel, we're talking from -- during the period from 13th of April to 17th of May. So your initial six weeks you were in theatre, more than half of your stay you had no contact whatsoever with Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned in your examination-in-chief that you had been given an org chart which mentioned a unit as having foreign elements in it.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And am I correct in saying that this is the extent of the information you possessed concerning the foreign elements in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, not fully. That's part of the information, and the rest of the information was given by fellow monitors that mentioned the 7th Muslim Brigade, that mentioned possible Mujahedins to me. So that fit together with the org chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, this incident that you mention - because I have your statement here, where it says that it was mentioned to you by a fellow monitor that there was a dangerous area with 7 Brigade - and if I recall correctly our conversation yesterday, this was the junction where you can either turn right and go to the southern part of Zenica or turn left and go towards Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you were basically told don't turn right and you never did turn right and go to that area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right. Since Zenica was never my responsibility, there was no reason for me to go to that district.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I -- the information that you do possess, then, is this incident that was mentioned to you by a colleague and the org chart that you were given, and we discussed last night you were also -- the issue of Mujahedin or foreign elements was also mentioned in meetings of local commissions at which the HVO was always present.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct. At several meetings of local joint commissions sometimes the HVO made allegations of foreign units or sometimes they even mentioned the word "Mujahedin." And they blamed atrocities committed by the Mujahedins.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I -- going through, in terms of this information, can you confirm that you yourself do not have any firsthand knowledge of either the Mujahedin or 7 Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct, no firsthand knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: On the 28th of May, in your statement you report a meeting at which the SDA and the HDZ presidency it was mentioned that both the 7 Brigade and 17 Brigade were under control of 3rd Corps, and this was mentioned to you by the politicians present and not by the military members present; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That was supposed to be the 1st of May, this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The 28th of May.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The 28th of May. So that was the meeting in Travnik, one of the preparation meetings for the provincial government.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this was the mayor of Travnik, Curic, who mentioned that both 7 and 17 Brigade were under control of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't recall whether Curic said that himself, but I have it in my notes and I can confirm who exactly stated this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, can you confirm that with respect to Mr. Merdan who was present at that meeting, that neither Mr. Merdan or anyone else, looking in your notes, ever told you that the Mujahedin were -- had anything to do with the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: You asked me that last night as well. I checked it last night. I couldn't find any evidence where Mr. Merdan or Mr. Alagic mentioned Mujahedin as being part of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like to show you, Colonel, a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like the usher to please distribute this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Colonel, I would like to draw your attention to the first document in the series of documents that was just handed to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I see my colleague is standing up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution objects to the first -- at least the first document in this bundle, and I would like to address the Trial Chamber in the absence of the witness, if I might, on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Colonel, you will have to leave the courtroom for a few minutes, and we will call you back as soon as possible. The usher will escort you out of the courtroom, and I will call you back in a few minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has previously objected to this document being shown to witnesses. We renew our objection based on the fact that a proper foundation hasn't necessarily been laid with respect to putting this information before this witness. There are references to a number of documents in this first tab of this material. There's also a number of items, including numbers 5 through 8 of this document, that occur outside the time frame when this witness was in Central Bosnia. I also note for the record that as we indicated previously, issue number 8 should be 1994, rather than 2004. There's also information contained in this document which appears to be testimony of prior witnesses, and again, the Prosecution has repeatedly objected to testimony of one witness being put before another witness when the, in effect, citation to the person who said that statement is included in the information rather than simply being a generic statement, without attribution to a particular individual. Again, I -- the Prosecution would assert, as it has in the past, that this document really should not be shown to witnesses, particularly because of the time element involved, in terms of information outside the scope of this witness's time in Central Bosnia, and also because there are indications in here of what other witnesses have said, and the Prosecution does not believe that's a proper way of putting these type of questions to this witness. In other words, there are other ways of doing this, Mr. President, which do not involve a Defence summary of the evidence, if you will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, you have heard the Prosecution's objection. They have listed a number of reasons for which they are making this objection. First of all, it concerns the date. The witness was only in the field for three months, and this document contains dates that don't fall within the period of time that he spent there. There are references to testimony received from other individuals, and the witness is not familiar with this. And the Prosecution also says that it might be possible to follow a different type of procedure. We could present documents from 2 to 5 and then base your questions on these documents.
