So why do you want to tender document number 1, which is a document that you yourself have drafted?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In fact, it was just to save time. Mr. President, each paragraph in this document refers to -- or relates to a document tendered before the Chamber. The Trial Chamber could take each individual document and have the witness read them out and then ask the witness questions, but this is a procedure that could take more than 30 minutes. We want to proceed in this manner because the witness said he had information about the Mujahedin being within the 3rd Corps. If the witness has information he can inform the Trial Chamber of with regard to this subject, it is important for the Defence to show the witness that he didn't have all the information, and this would enable him to amend or change his opinion. So there are two ways in which I could proceed: Either I can use this document and add references to various documents and their numbers, or I could just use this document - that would save time - and then my colleague, if he thinks that the paragraphs in this document don't accurately reflect the documents that have been tendered, in that case my colleague could argue his case and make the relevant submissions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence would like to follow this procedure in order to save time: Document number 1 adopts elements from document number 2, and the Defence says that the Prosecution could always contest any given point in the paragraph. There are two ways of proceeding: There is the lengthy procedure we could follow; we would present the witness with an official document and then ask the witness questions. And there is another more rapid procedure, which would enable us to save time. So that is the crux of the matter. What is your opinion of this, Mr. Mundis? Naturally, you can always keep paragraph 1 under control, because if the Prosecution misrepresents anything, you can always raise an objection. You can always state your position. What is your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President the Prosecution would submit that a quicker way to do this was to actually ask the witness questions about whether he was aware of any letters from the commander of the 3rd Corps going up the chain of command concerning the Mujahedin or the foreign fighters. In the event the witness says he's not aware of that, and two or three questions would probably solve that, that would seem to be the end of it. We have a whole series of events, as the Defence has characterised it, that this witness is most likely not going to know anything about whatsoever, and by showing him this two-page document that includes testimony of other witnesses, this actually, the Prosecution submits, might lengthen the entire proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will withdraw for a few minutes to deliberate. --- Break taken at 11.47 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After having deliberated and in light of the objection raised, the Trial Chamber believes that the Defence should show the witness documents 2 to 5. The witness will recognise these documents, because they come from the European mission that he was a part of. And then on the basis of these documents you can ask the witness the questions that you formulated more or less in document number 1. But show him the documents, have him identify the documents, and then ask the witness the questions. It will take a little longer perhaps, but it would be more appropriate to proceed in this manner. It will amount to the same thing, but it will take a little longer. Madam Usher, could you call the witness back into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to the fact that the documents, which are in a bundle and which were provided to the witness, are not the documents referenced in the first document. These are different documents. They're new documents. The Trial Chamber has never seen them and they haven't been admitted into evidence. So the first document is a summary of documents that have been tendered. What I suggest to do, Mr. President, is to show the witness the first document and then to proceed orally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead. You may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could the usher please show the witness document DH73.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] Colonel, before you look at this document, I would like to ask you a few questions and then we will move on to looking at this specific document. First I would like to confirm, just to come back on one of your answers a little earlier concerning the information that was provided to you by your colleague with respect to the fact that there might be a dangerous area not to go to and not to make this right turn at the Busovaca junction. Now, I read here from your statement, where it says that -- it says here in your statement: "I joined RC Zenica. I was warned by my colleagues to avoid a southern district of the city because it was home to the 7 Muslim Brigade, which was considered to be very hostile to the international community." Would you agree that there is no mention of Mujahedin whatsoever in the information that was provided to you by your colleague but they were talking about 7 Brigade only?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It's not literally stated in that part of the testimony before, but what I do recall in my memory is that my fellow -- some of my fellow monitors not only told me about the 7th Muslim Brigade but also told me about Mujahedins being part of -- being members of this 7th Muslim Brigade. It might not be in that text. But what I recall from my memory is that there was a relationship between the 7th Muslim Brigade and the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you yourself, Colonel, in terms of looking at the Mujahedin, you don't know where the Mujahedin came from.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you don't know when they arrived in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you don't know where they were -- they physically were in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right; I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you don't know either what financial resources they had and where they took their money.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you don't know, Colonel, what links, if any, they had with religious leaders.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you don't know what and -- what kind and how many weapons they had.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you don't know what their fighting doctrine was or any fighting methods.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Not literally what the doctrine was, but based on the allegations, I was told that these Mujahedins were used to threaten people, to -- let's say to do limited actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, I need to bring you back to one of your previous answers concerning the fact that what kind and how many weapons they had. You had no information to that effect; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to go to this Exhibit Number DH73 and to please take the time to read this letter. Colonel, do you agree that this is a letter which appears to have been written by General Hadzihasanovic to his superior headquarters posing a number of questions but basically that deals with the Mujahedins?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Can I see the bottom, please. I confirm that it's a letter from the 13th of June - at least, it's a typed-out letter apparently - and the name of Mr. Hadzihasanovic is on the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the first paragraph of this letter, it talks about the fact that in the area of Zenica since the beginning of war there had been volunteers and -- as well as a group of Bosnians trained by them and that these people have not entered the ranks of the Bosnian army, in spite of being invited to do so.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you agree with this information -- not that it's the truth, but that what this information actually says is that there is a group of people that are foreign elements and that are not in the army.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's what it says in this letter, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that these people do not want -- I refer you to the end of the paragraph, for the sake of time -- "wish to communicate exclusively with top officials of the army staff and not with the 3rd Corps commander."

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's that it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that they believe that the duty of the corps commander is to arrange a meeting with these people and that's it. Is that what this letter appears to say?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the second paragraph, that these people had been fighting outside the usual context and lawful methods of combat and that these are directly detrimental to both the state and to the army. And that it is a known fact that they have links to state organs and high-ranking Muslim clergymen. Do you agree that this is what this letter says?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you -- if I refer you to the last paragraph, where it says: "I am requesting your stances and opinions regarding the solution to this problem, because these units are situated in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, and I do not want to be held accountable...." You had no information whatsoever about the existence of this letter, did you?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I mention to you that this letter was actually reported into a milinfosum, would that mean that you did not read the milinfosum that day?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It depends on if it's a UN military information summary or if it's a ECMM one. Normally these ECMM information summaries were kept at the regional centre headquarters, and important information from these summaries normally would be briefed during -- either morning briefings or evening briefings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I must say I did not attend all those briefings since I was not every night in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say, Colonel, that these milinfosums prepared by the British Battalion, as well as the ECMM reports, they were available within the Regional Centre Zenica but that you did not always read them because you had lots of things to do?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, yesterday I mentioned to you something about an order being issued by the army headquarters to General Hadzihasanovic, and I'd like to ask you if you knew any information about such an order asking General Hadzihasanovic to send these foreign elements to Mount Igman to work with an army asset, an independent unit which was attached directly to the army and not to the 3rd Corps, and that if they refused to show them no hospitality and to disarm them? Did you have any information concerning this order?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, I did not. I was informed by you last night for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I ask you whether you have any information that upon receiving this order, General Hadzihasanovic in the telephone conversation which was triggered by army headquarters basically opposed this order on the basis that for him he could not disarm the Mujahedin using force because this would be the same as opening a third front, did you have any information concerning this specific telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I could show you many more documents, but would you agree with me - because now we are entering an area where you are away from Bosnia, because you left on 13th of July; right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you agree that the information you had on the Mujahedin was actually very scarce and that in fact you knew nothing about all the measures undertaken by the 3rd Corps to try and solve the Mujahedin problem?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right, yes, I knew very little of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if I suggest to you, Colonel - and I call now on your military experience - that if I tell you that it may have appeared that an option for General Hadzihasanovic would have been to disarm them with force - I put this to you as a scenario - would you agree with me that if we want to analyse or to second-guess the decision of General Hadzihasanovic not to use force to disarm the Mujahedin, that in order for anyone to be able to second-guess this decision, we would need the following information: Would you agree that we would need some information with respect to the resources available to General Hadzihasanovic at the time?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yeah, that sounds fair. If you want to judge or to decide about something, you need more information to be able to estimate what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you agree that we would also need some information on basically the status of play at that specific time? And namely, in this case you are aware of what was the status with the front line against the Serbs and what was the status of play in the conflict between the HVO and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina inside the area of the 3rd Corps, and that we would need to assess this to be able to know if we have the luxury of taking on or disarming the Mujahedin by force.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yeah, sounds logical. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you also agree that it would be necessary - and this would probably be the first thing any military analyst would do - and that is to determine who the Mujahedin were in terms of their numbers, their location, the weapons they have, and their resources, and that this is the basics for any military commander about to launch an attack?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you also agree that before a corps commander could launch such an attack opening a third front against a different enemy, he would have to obtain the consent from his superior headquarters?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: If the effect would always be a third front, yes, then you need the approval of the third -- of your superior commander. If it's just an internal matter in your own area of responsibility, I wouldn't ask for permission; I would feel myself responsible and do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it depends on the circumstances of the situation.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It does, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me, Colonel that, in order to evaluate or assess the decision of General Hadzihasanovic, it is necessary to have all of the information that we've just outlined?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, at least to be able to estimate it you need additional information and you have to thoroughly weigh this information and to decide on it based on this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like to move now to another area, Colonel, and that is the issue of the joint operation headquarters. Can you confirm that the joint operational headquarters was created on the 5th of May and that it was located in the basement of the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact date, but it was early May. I think it took some time until it was really effective, so depends on what you call the creation. I think the decision was made maybe a bit earlier, but becoming effective took at least a week, I think, or one and a half week, and it was situated in the basement of the PTT building in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now, can you -- in terms of this joint operational headquarters, can you confirm that this was the result of a decision taken at the highest level, namely between President Izetbegovic on behalf of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and his counterpart from the HVO side?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: You told me last night that this is the case. I must say I was not aware of the fact that Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Tudjman were dealing with this personally. I was aware that high-level politicians supported this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I would not want, Colonel, to be -- to mislead anyone in terms of providing you with information, but my question more to you is: Are you aware that it is the result of a decision at the highest level?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right. I was aware of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Without me telling you anything.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. I was clearly told and I knew and I experienced the -- let's say the top-level support for this joint command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the joint command itself, you remember the cease-fire which was agreed by both commanders, do you?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I do, yes. Late April, that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you also remember the fact that there were some communication problems which led to the necessity to transport the commander around so that he could address the troops personally with respect to the cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right. And this complaint of lack of communications was made in the early days of the cease-fire several times. And that led to the decision of both commanders, Mr. Halilovic and Mr. Petkovic, with support of the British Battalion with armoured vehicles in the company of EC monitors, to visit certain hot spots at the front lines. And we did so at the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the cease-fire, would you agree with me that this cease-fire was putting a term prayer hold -- temporary hold on the operations that were following the Ahmici massacre?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Well, it was not stated in that way that it's supposed to be a temporary hold. It was stated as a cease-fire, and the basis for further negotiations maybe to withdraw or to set a new status quo or whatever. But I didn't see it as a temporary hold. Not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, Colonel, would you agree with me that at this particular time at the end of April the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was moving back on the offensive and they were basically in a very good military posture at that time the cease-fire was declared?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I think that depends on the level in which you estimate the situation and it depends on the local situation. For instance, the part of Old Vitez was encircled. So that was not a got situation. If you look at it from the wider perspective, you could argue that the Lasva Valley was encircled. So it depends on the perspective you take.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, Colonel that, there was incredible restraint displayed by the commanders on the army -- on the side of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina to stop their troops who were very angered by the Ahmici massacre?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I agree that both sides put restraints on their local commanders, and I can see that the Ahmici massacre upset a lot of people. More than upset them. I can see that. But the relation is -- I can understand that there is a relation, but I can't prove it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I'd like to move on to another area, and that is dealing with the Travnik church. Can you confirm that you did not visit the Travnik church?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I did not enter the Travnik church. I lived in the Hotel Orient quite close to the church, so I saw the church several times. I went by it. I heard the bells ringing. But I didn't enter it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you can also attest to the fact that you had some dealings nevertheless with the priest --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- with the priest who was responsible for this church.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you cannot remember, Colonel, any significant damage done to the church; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct. I didn't see any damage personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in your statement, it is noted that you briefly noted in your notebook that probably homes and church were shot at but that there was no significant damage.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It's not clear from that page what church is referred to. If it is the Travnik church, I visited Travnik several times in that time frame and I didn't see any damage. But there were more Catholic churches in that region. The Dolac church was apparently hit by a mortar shell or an artillery shell, so that had some damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you remember saying in your statement, Colonel, that "the church bell continued to call worshippers to mass throughout this period" so that the church must have been able to continue functioning?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. I recall the church bells ringing several times, but I don't know exactly what was the last time that I heard these bells ringing or what was the last time that I went by this church. So that was certainly not the 13th of July when I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you also say in your statement that on the 18th of June the HVO claimed that the church had been robbed and damaged and you are of the understanding that someone from the ECMM did follow up this claim.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right. To my recollection, Mr. Watkins, Philip Watkins, he even made a special report on the situation of churches in the wider area of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I move on to another area, Colonel, I'd like to address the issue of Guca Gora. Can you confirm, Colonel, that on the night of the 7th to 8th of June you were -- you spent the night in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that waking up at 6.30 you heard the sound of heavy fighting in the Travnik area?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I heard it then already from the Travnik area. I heard in Zenica the sounds of artillery in the distance. So that struck me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And yourself and Mr. Watkins, another ECMM colleague, drove first to the headquarters of the HVO in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that from what you could see from the HVO headquarters, they were in a real panic and they made wild claims that Guca Gora was in flames and that civilians had been massacred. Do you recall this event?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I recall that they were in a panic-like situation. I wouldn't call it "wild claims." They made allegations, claims that Guca Gora was in flames, set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you also recall that later on you drove to Nova Bila to the church, where you saw many wounded people, most from the HVO, and that again you heard these allegations about Guca Gora being in flames?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, Colonel, that later it turned out that the smoke the Croats had seen actually came from burning houses in Bandol?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, as an aside to this question, I would like you to confirm, Colonel, if you can, that in the three months you spent in Central Bosnia the only two towns where you saw extensive destruction beyond battle damage in the area of 3 Corps are Ahmici and Bandol and no other towns.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: In the Lasva Valley, that's correct. I saw more signs of this, like in the area of Kiseljak, but as you explained to me yesterday, that's outside the 3rd Corps area. So for the 3rd Corps area, that's correct. Ahmici was the worst example, and Bandol, being a smaller village, was similar, burnt and damaged like Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In both of these villages, all -- the extensive destruction was done to Muslim property.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: What I could tell from the shape of the houses, yes, I guess it was Muslim property.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the damage you even report from the Kiseljak area, even though it is not in the area of the 3rd Corps, was also damage done to Muslim property.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, yourself and Mr. Watkins, just to look at this specific incident, because there were of course allegations, can you confirm that you immediately went to the headquarters of General Alagic in Travnik to inquire about the situation?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that you asked permission to General Alagic to go to Guca Gora and that not only did he agree but he decided to come along and to bring two members of the HVO, as well as a priest.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct. I must say the priest was, as I recall it, not his initiative, but he agreed that we took the priest with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And without saying the name, can you also confirm that there was a representative of the UNHCR who also went along with you.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether she -- whether this representative was already there on the first day when we visited Guca Gora. I'm very positive that this representative was there on the second day, when we arranged the evacuation of the citizens from Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived in Guca Gora with General Alagic and the other members of the delegation, you can confirm, General -- Colonel, sorry, that the monastery was not on fire.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that you did not notice any significant damage to the houses nearby the monastery.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you also saw that there were somewhere around 200 civilians sheltering in the monastery.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you actually spoke to these people.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: To some of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And these people reported damage to neighbouring villages but none of them had seen any damage.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I haven't seen the damage myself. I don't recall that those people didn't see the damage themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You know, however, that the British Battalion sent out a recce patrol and that they found four or five bodies but no evidence of a massacre.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you stayed, yourself and Mr. Watkins, for about an hour or so before you returned to Zenica, but first taking a badly injured man with you.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right. And we treated him in the Nova Bila hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the next day you once again returned to Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And on that day your colleague Junhov was there as well as this representative of the UNHCR, as well as the commander of the British Battalion.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at that occasion you debated the politics of whether you should or should not evacuate the civilians who were in the monastery.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: We took part in this debate or discussion. It was not our first responsibility. I think the UNHCR had the priority in this, and of course they needed support and advice from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And on that day, Colonel, General Alagic was not there but Mr. Merdan was there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you confirm concerning General Alagic that on more than one occasion he basically said that there was no reason for this, that the Croats could stay, that they would be protected, and that they should be able to stay where they are?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I recall that he stated that several times for the wider Travnik area. I'm not sure whether he referred to Guca Gora itself, but there was still at that time some 5.000 Croats living in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned, Colonel, in your statement the name of a Mr. Sipic as being a local commander of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that he was present when talking about the possibility to evacuate the civilians.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: As I recall it, Mr. Sipic was the responsible brigade commander for that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you recall, Colonel, that Mr. Sipic opposed the evacuation of the Croat civilians on the basis that there was no need for them to depart and that he could ensure their safety.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct. But in the end, he gave in and he agreed with a safe evacuation of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And then those civilians were taken to Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. First we had to organise the transport, of course. The British Battalion took care of that, with a large number of Warriors, armoured vehicles, some small armoured vehicles, and some trucks. We escorted them along the mountain road. We were stopped on that road, had to do some negotiations again, and finally brought the people to Nova Bila and to -- I'm not sure what the town is called. I think Bila on the main road, parallel to the Lasva River.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, can you confirm that after spending two days, not full-time but two days in a row you were in Guca Gora, that other than for the fact that maybe you know which unit Mr. Sipic belonged to, you do not know which units were on the parting in the area in Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I did not see any fighting or soldiers in Guca Gora. The only, let's say, soldiers on duty we encountered was at several checkpoints close to Mosor, where at that time there was still fighting going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in the two days you were in Guca Gora, you never saw anyone that you could describe as being a Mujahedin, did you?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like to refer you to the bundle of documents which was provided to you, simply to look at a picture that we have in there. And I would like you to -- this is the fifth document in the bundle that was provided to you. Do you recognise, Colonel, this picture?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I do, yes. I have the original with me. It's my picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You have the original with you?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you mind using the original and to put it on the ELMO, please. Can you describe, Colonel, this picture for the benefit of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: What you see here is the monastery in Guca Gora with two British armoured vehicles in front of it and three British soldiers standing at the back of one of the Warrior vehicles. This picture was, as I recall, taken by myself with my own camera on the 8th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I don't know if it's the quality of the picture, but is it possible for the usher maybe to play around with the lighting, just because there appears to be some -- do you see, Colonel, this, like, kind of shaded area on the picture itself? Is that a true picture, or is this something -- is this just the sun?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I think it's only the shining of the light on the ELMO. The picture itself is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And last night when you showed me this picture, Colonel, you indicated to me that -- I'm not sure if it's this specific picture, but you could see from the distance Bandol and the smoke coming out of Bandol.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's the second picture, but I must point out that the name of this representative of UNHCR is written underneath this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Underneath it?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: So if you don't want show this name then you have to cover it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Underneath, like below?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can I ask the usher to show this picture but to hide the names that on this second picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you indicate, Colonel, what this picture is and when it was taken?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: This was taken the same day and shows the same vehicle that was in the previous picture, the same Warrior vehicle. Now from the other side we are looking southwards towards the mountains in the direction of the Lasva Valley. And what I make of this is smoke in the background on the horizon. And if you look at the map, you can make out that this must be smoke coming from houses of Bandol. Standing from the back of the vehicle is the liaison officer, without the helmet; there is this UNHCR representative from the back, and there is facing towards me -- I think it was the battalion second-in-command or maybe the company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Could you indicate with a pointer, Colonel, where you see the smoke on the picture, because the picture might not be very clear.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: This is a pile of smoke. This is a pile of smoke. And this is some smoke over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, regarding these two photographs, we would like to tender them into evidence. However, the witness wants to keep the photos, so we would like to take the photos to photocopy them and to tender photocopies into evidence at that stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, do you have any objections to the photos that the witness took himself and has recognised as his own?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, nor do we have any objection to photocopies being substituted for the original photos so that the witness can maintain his own originals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're going to give us the photos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. I am looking at the time. I still need a couple minutes and -- ten minutes, and after the break I'm going to finish, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to make a break. It is half past 12.00. And we are going to resume at five to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, you may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Colonel, I just have a few more questions for you. And to begin, I would like to turn to your testimony in the Blaskic case and ask you whether you confirm some of the answers you provided on that occasion. My first question deals with the fact that the HVO and the political entities of the Bosnian Croat side used propaganda to incite fear in the minds of Croats who were residing in areas held by Bosnian Muslims and that that resulted in a large movement of Croat civilians from those areas. And the question which was put to you in reference to these facts was: "Could you explain to the Judges your views on that question and can you also cite some examples." And your response was initially that "The HVO used propaganda using radio and television, both HDZ and also HVO." Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the propaganda, there was one event where it was indicated that in Zenica there had been a number of Croats killed and that this proved out to be totally unfounded. Can you recall these events?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I mention to you this quote here that comes from your response, where you mention: "On the radio, on the Croatian radio it was stated and explained that a large group of Croatians had been killed in Zenica and that therefore these people could not return and be safe in their homes. The radio also stated that it would no longer be safe for these people to go to Nova Bila and to Vitez." And you add: "That's not correct. It would be safer for them to go to Nova Bila and to Vitez." Would you agree with me that the radio, the HVO -- sorry, the Croatian radio, what the radio was actually saying is it would be safer for the refugees not to return to their homes in Muslim-held territory but to go to HVO-held territory?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: With respect to Guca Gora, a question was asked to you in terms of -- and I quote the question: "Can you tell the Judges the exact nature of the propaganda that you were aware of that attempted to get the Croat population from returning from their homes?" And basically your answer was: "It was explained to me that the propaganda consisted of stating that a large number of Croatians or Croats, rather, had been assassinated. This was in the Zenica region. The propaganda stated that a large number of houses had been burned. It also stated that other houses had been looted and that the Mujahedin had the intention to exterminate the remaining Croats." And a question that was put to you was: "Based on the result of your investigation, that was grossly exaggerated." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to move on, Colonel, to -- again to the bundle of documents which was given to you and to document number 2 in this bundle. Can you confirm that this is a document which is dated 1 June of 1993 and that this is a report that was prepared by yourself, Mr. Watkins, and Mr. Kinigopoulos?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I refer you to the first paragraph of this document talking about the situation in Travnik. Can you recall the incident whereby the commander of the Operational Group Bosanska Krajina was in fact arrested and stopped and robbed by HVO elements?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I do recall that. Although I was not present myself, I do recall the incidents, since we met Mr. Alagic later on that evening, when he complained about it and when he asked us to negotiate in taking measures for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, Colonel, that an incident like this, where the commander of an operational group, which is somewhat like a division in your language, is a very significant event that can really lead to disastrous consequences?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I now refer you to the document labeled as number 3 in the bundle. Can you confirm that the first page of this document is dated 8 June 1993?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that the author of this document appears to be Jean-Pierre Thebault?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you know Jean-Pierre Thebault as being Ambassador Thebault, the head of RC Zenica.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you by looking at the next two pages confirm that the next two pages are actually your report, drafted on the 8th of June, along with Mr. Watkins?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if I just refer you to the first page. Do you recall Ambassador Thebault putting this cover page on your report?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't recall the act, but I know that he did, since I have the originals in my possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I refer you to the second paragraph, where it says: "If the BH -- BiH army attack is clear, it seems also to be now clear that the allegations of atrocities or ethnic cleansing made by the Bosnian Croats are intentionally exaggerated when not completely false. It is not the less disturbing that what is presented as the reactions of a panicked population was announced three days ago by the HVO officials of Travnik." Is that information that you can recall, in terms of the existence of this information?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I can. And I know that Mr. Thebault wrote this, addressing the headquarters in -- in Zagreb, and he explained this, let's say, introduction letter on the basis of information that he got from Mr. Watkins and from me myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I now refer you to the fourth document under -- that was provided to you. Can you please confirm, Colonel, that this document dated 19th of June of 1993, labeled as a "Follow-up report on the Travnik situation" follows the same pattern where there is a cover letter drafted by Ambassador Thebault followed by a special report dated 8 June -- oh, sorry, this is the same one -- 19 June. Sorry, 19 June. Yes, the 19th of June. And then -- which of course includes your report 8 June once again?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct. It's not exactly the same, this attachment, since in the first attachment Watkins and me have signed and in the second attachment it's Watkins and Junhov.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes. Also dated the 8th of June.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I'd like you to answer a few questions with respect to Mr. Alagic. In terms of -- you can confirm that in your view Mr. Alagic was both a professional officer who was respected by his soldiers but he was also a very proud but very fair. Would you agree with this assessment?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that General Alagic always was accessible, tried to be helpful in providing you with the necessary authorisation, and that at no time you never had the impression that he was hiding anything from you?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: He was very accessible to me. I cannot state that he was always accessible, but to me he was. Sometimes I had to wait for 15 minutes, maybe once half an hour, if he was very busy. But he never sent us or my fellow monitors away without addressing us personally, and he showed his willingness in even going on the ground himself with us, accompanying us. And he also accepted suggestions made by the ECMM to escort people from one location to the other or to give freedom of movement to certain numbers of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to refer you, Colonel, to one specific example which you said in the Blaskic trial, and I'd like you to confirm whether this is still your views today. And it says here: "I remember that once after the incident in Guca Gora, that we had to go and visit General Alagic and report these accusations, saying that in the Guca Gora church several weeks before, certain sacred objects had been damaged." And you go on to say that "General Alagic was impressed by the accusations. He apologised immediately and said to us immediately that he would have this kind of activity stopped immediately and that he would attempt to track down the guilty parties in order to punish them."

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I recall that. It was somewhere in the second part of June, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And a question was also put to you in the same context in terms of comparing the degree of damage done to Catholic religious sites in Muslim-held territory versus the amount of damage done to Muslim religious sites in HVO-held territory. Would you confirm this response as still being your views today: "The Catholic objects were practically never damaged. I saw one minor example in a Catholic church near Busovaca. There was a little bit of damage to the church. I saw many examples of mosques, minarets, including others in Ahmici, where the mosque and minaret had been completely destroyed. This also happened in other places. The ratio between the damage to Catholic buildings as opposed to Muslim buildings was something really that one cannot say was even comparable." Do you recall this answer?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I recall it, and that was my experience at that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I indicate to you that -- or suggest to you that in fact - and you may not be aware of this information - but if I suggest to you that General Alagic did in fact take numerous disciplinary measures and initiated numerous criminal reports, would that be of surprise to you, knowing the man?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No. Numerous sounds a bit too general to me, but I accept that he -- and I would expect from him that he would take measures, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe if I make my question more precise. I'm not saying there was. I'm saying if there were, would that be consistent with what you have seen from General Alagic?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It would be consistent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I move on to Mr. Merdan. You mentioned that he was a senior figure within the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that you dealt regularly with him because of his role in the Busovaca Joint Commission.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You said that he was professional, easy-going, and that he was able to arrange free passage.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, on one specific occasion on the 19th of May, you attended a meeting that is reported in your statement, where you say that "during the meeting Merdan told his commanders not to blame lapses on third parties or uncontrollable elements and to take responsibility for their actions." Do you recall this specific moment of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It was a meeting in -- I think in Han Bila where a brigade and some battalion commanders of the local military units were together in the joint commission, and we had met a few days before. We made agreements, and Merdan quite clearly told them that they should be effective and they should live up to those agreements and make it possible for both the commanders themselves and for the commission to do their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did Mr. Merdan on this specific occasion appear to you to be sincere and true or something else?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: He appeared to be sincere and true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in your own understanding of what he was saying, was he referring to 3rd Corps policy and Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina policy?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that, but he was present in the meeting before and he was present when we made those arrangements, and he was a deputy commander with enough authority to, I'd say, sign up officially for those agreements, so he could order his subordinates to follow up these agreements. So he was in the position to make comments on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, Colonel, you may not be aware of this, but once again, if I suggest to you that within the 3rd Corps headquarters numerous disciplinary measures were taken and numerous criminal reports were filed -- again, you may not know this. But if that is the case, would that be consistent with your knowledge and your perception of Mr. Merdan and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It would be consistent with my knowledge of Mr. Merdan, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Last question, Colonel: Would you agree with me that when looking at the HVO, that they were better looking, they had better uniforms, they had better equipment, but that they had also much more problems with them, especially at checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: "Better looking" sounds a bit strange for soldiers. I mean, as soldiers with their outfit, in that that sense, it was better military looking. It's hard to give a general conclusion about problems at checkpoints. There were various checkpoints, really numerous checkpoints, and some of them never gave us problems; some others sometimes did when there was fighting going on. And there were other checkpoints where we always had problems. I think problems at HVO checkpoints occurred more than at Armija BiH checkpoints, in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, having spent three months in Central Bosnia, can you attest to the difficult situation in which the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was placed in, looking at, first, the extensive front line with the Serbs that they have to man? Or did you witness this?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Can you explain the word "attest"?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Could you -- well, simply confirm that they had a very long front line to man against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: There was a very large front line, but it was not only the Armija BiH side. As I experienced it or as they explained it to me, it was a mutual arrangement between HVO units and Armija BiH units fighting side by side opposing the Serb army, the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And are you aware, Colonel, that towards the early June, the HVO literally walked out from the front line, leaving all of the responsibility to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I saw and heard reports of that by the British forces, and I heard statements from Mr. Alagic himself about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that this would create necessarily big problems for any commander involved with such a situation.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You were also aware, Colonel, about the difficulty of roads being blocked and that, as a matter of fact, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina being sort of in a siege, in terms of being limited to Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: If you take a very wide perspective, yes, they were encircled in Bosnia. And I see the need for free lines of communications from a military perspective.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in a shorter scale, you can also confirm that Zenica was regularly the object of shelling.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct. I experienced that myself several times, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that the shelling can really disrupt the activity that is going on in Zenica, whether it be civilian, commercial, or military.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It could, but it was not on a regular basis. Sometimes three shells fell in a few minutes and sometimes several days there was no shelling at all. So I do not agree that it will stop all public and military life. Life has to go on, and especially military life has to go on, so you won't be stopped by incidentally shelling or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you would agree that it is a factor that disrupts the activity.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my colleague referred a question to you concerning the tempo of operations. I would simply try to put an image for the Judges. Can you confirm that you yourself, not being part of one of the warring factions, not having to face an enemy that could kill you, and being there only for three months, without having your family there being endangered by the shelling, that you had not one minute to spare during the three months that you were there?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I took some minutes to spare, but it was a very busy time and I had to deal with eight, up to ten different commanders altogether -- with my fellow monitors, of course. I didn't do the work all by myself. But I must say I also -- and with me and the other monitors we had to drive to be as effective as possible -- to drive to use every minute we had and not to take a break, although I had a few days' break on the coastline. So this busyness was also due to the drive we had to solve problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you confirm, as a last question, Colonel, that tempo of operations is one thing, but that the activities you were involved in were non-stop and that when there is operations at a high tempo your activities may change, but even when the tempo of operations diminishes, there were other types of activities for you to do and when you were every day busy, it was hectic times and we're talking 20 hours a day?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that this went on for all your colleagues at ECMM?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I guess it should. But I don't think everyone was as motivated, so you should take it individually. The majority of the monitors were very, very, very busy, and some others were not that busy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This concludes the cross-examination on behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the documents are concerned, what are you requesting? With regard to number 2, 3, and 4, what is your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to tender documents 2, 3, 4, and 5 into evidence. And with the assistance of the registrar, we now have a colour copy of the two photographs presented by the witness. So, Mr. President, I would like documents 2, 3, 4, and 5 to be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness should write down his name on the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I'll ask the usher to give these documents to the witness so that he can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution has no objection to these three documents and two photographs being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would just like to point out that we have a French translation of document 2; we have a full translation of this document -- I apologise, we have a full translation for document number 3 and we have a partial French translation of document number 4. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have exhibit numbers for these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the ECMM daily summary report dated 1st of June, 1993 gets the exhibit number DH184, and its French translation gets the exhibit number DH184/F. The ECMM special report on Travnik dated 8th of June, 1993 gets the exhibit number DH185, and its French translation gets the exhibit number DH185/F. The ECMM report dated 19th of June, 1993 gets the exhibit number DH186, and its French translation gets the exhibit number DH186/F. The set of two photographs of Guca Gora gets the exhibit number DH187.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the document dated the 1st of June -- 184, doesn't -- we don't have a French version for it. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon, will you take the floor or will your colleague do so? As you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, if I could refer you, first of all, to a meeting that you were taken to by my learned friend Mr. Bourgon on the 28th of May, 1993, where you were present and you said that at this meeting, which was a joint SDA/HDZ presidency meeting in Travnik on the 28th of May, 1993, that the mayor of Travnik stated that the 7th Brigade and the 17th Krajina Brigade were fully under control. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Do you also recall, as it's something which is stated in your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, that present at the meeting was General Alagic, who was then the commander of the OGBK, which was part of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And do you also recall that present at the meeting was the Chief of Staff of the Bosnian army, General Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. That's in my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: So not only were there civilian leaders present at the meeting with you there were also military leaders present, including leaders from the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Turning to the 7th Brigade in particular. It is correct, is it not, that Zenica was not within your area of responsibility; it was outside of your area that you took responsibility for?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It's hard to state it that way, because my area of responsibility changed now and then, but my main area of responsibility lied in Vitez, Busovaca, Kiseljak, and Travnik. Occasionally I went to Tarcin, I went to Grahovcici, and I went to Bugojno once.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And those places and towns that you've mentioned now, they would have been the focus of your work and what you took responsibility for; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: So it would be correct, would it not, that you had no reason to and indeed you did not yourself verify or seek to check out any of the allegations that were made about the 7th Brigade, which you said to us today were told to you by other people?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct. Normally allegations made concerning another area of responsibility were reported either in the evening briefing sessions in the ECMM or they were mentioned in a daily report and then the staff of the ECMM used to appoint another monitor or a team of monitors to check on it, or the other party - for instance, the HVO or the Armija BiH - checked on it and then reported in the next meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you. So in respect to the matters that were mentioned about the 7th Brigade, it was not your responsibility to follow any of those matters up that you heard about. Those were the responsibility of others?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And likewise, you therefore had no reason and you did not at any stage visit the 7th Brigade headquarters or barracks that were situated in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct. I did not visit them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have just a couple of questions for the witness, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, my learned colleague for the Defence asked you about a meeting on the 19th of May, 1993 when Mr. Merdan told his commanders to take responsibility for their actions and not to blame lapses on third parties or uncontrollable elements. You remember that meeting?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know what he was referring to with respect to "third parties or uncontrollable elements"?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Not that I recall now. I can look it up in the notes to refresh my memory. Maybe that gives more clarity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'll move on, sir. The Defence also showed you a document from General Hadzihasanovic to General Delic concerning, again, foreign elements in the 3rd Corps AOR. Do you remember seeing that document?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I remember seeing it here in this court, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you'd told us you'd never seen that document before.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall at any of the commission meetings where the subject of foreign fighters was raised by one of the parties?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. It was raised several times, but maybe in a matter that has to be explained. Sometimes foreign units were mentioned as units not belonging to a certain area of responsibility, for instance, a brigade belonging to the Travnik area assisting forces in the Vitez area, for instance. So that could be a foreign unit. If they were addressing foreign fighters or Mujahedins, that was quite clear that they meant real foreigners, people from another country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, at any of those meetings where any commanders or leaders of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH conveyed information to you that was similar to that contained in the letter that the Defence showed you?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall at any of these meetings where any of the 3rd Corps or its subordinate commands, any of the leaders told you that the foreign fighters or Mujahedin were not under their control?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that they ever mentioned the Mujahedins themselves. They mentioned the 7th Muslim Brigade, and in my interpretation I see Mujahedins and the 7th Muslim Brigade as part of one entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, sir, did they ever at any point any leaders of the ABiH 3rd Corps indicate to you that the 7th Muslim Brigade was not under the 3rd Corps' command and control?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: In the beginning, I recall that Mr. Merdan stated that they tried to get control over this brigade and later on he stated that they had full control over it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, just a brief question from the Judges. To a question put to you by the Defence, you said that the Croatian radio was rife with propaganda. When you -- did you listen to the Croatian radio? How did you know that they broadcast propaganda?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I did not listen to the radio myself since I don't understand the language. It was told to me by our own interpreters and it was told to me by, amongst others, Father Stipan, a Catholic priest in Zenica, and it was told by representatives in Grahovcici and some other places, where they said that, "We listen to radio broadcasts and in these broadcasts people were advised to go to other areas based on information," and we were able to deny that information and that gave us the belief or the impression that these advices given by the radio were false or not correct or in fact used as propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreter that you had with you, who did the interpreter belong to?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: We had a large number of interpreters related to the ECMM headquarters in Zenica. The two female interpreters I worked with most were both from a Croat Catholic ethnicity, from a Croat Catholic background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was it possible for you to have Muslim interpreters as well?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, sir. We quite often used Muslim interpreters. Of course, the female interpreters had to take a break now and then. All together I worked regularly with a group of five or six interpreters out of a total number of, I think, ten interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. I am going to ask my fellow Judges whether there are any more questions from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any more questions from the Defence? If not, Colonel, your examination is about to finish. And as you can see, it didn't last for 20 hours, thanks to the Defence, who made their questions brief and up to the point. Thank you very much for coming to testify. You have answered the questions put to you by the Prosecution, by the Defence, and by the Judges. I wish you a good journey back home and a lot of success in your present position. I'm going to ask Madam Usher to accompany you out of the courtroom. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can we please go into private session. There's something that I need to address in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Benjamin has not come back. I hope she's not lost to this Tribunal. Can you please advise us of the schedule for tomorrow and then I'm going to give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I share your hope that Mrs. Benjamin is not lost. The witness that is on the schedule as previously provided to The Chamber and to the Defence will in fact be available to testify tomorrow. There are no additional changes to the schedule for this week, as set forth in the letter of last Friday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. I believe that Mr. Bourgon was on his feet. Do you want to intervene at this point, Mr. Bourgon? No. In that case, there are no issues to raise. I would like to thank everybody and I invite all of you to come back tomorrow at 9.00. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 26th day of May, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.40 p.m.,
